quantum_foundations.goal: A particle of mass m moves along a line through a potential V(x), and it is described not by a position but by a complex wave ψ(x, t). Write how that wave changes in time: the left side is iħ times its rate of change, the right side is the energy operator acting on it - kinetic energy from the curvature of ψ, plus the potential.
quantum_foundations.name: Time-dependent Schrödinger equation (one dimension)
quantum_foundations.ask: For V = 0 a plane wave e^{i(kx−ωt)} solves it with momentum p = ħk = mv, so its wavelength is λ = 2π/k = h/(mv). Find λ in nm for an electron, with h in units of 1e-34 J s, m in 1e-31 kg and v in 1e6 m/s (the unit factors combine to exactly 1 nm).
quantum_foundations.method: Kinetic energy is p²/2m with momentum acting as −iħ ∂/∂x, so p² becomes −ħ² ∂²/∂x²; add the potential energy as a multiplier.

chemical_bonding.goal: Two identical atoms A and B each hold one orbital, φ on A and χ on B. Try the shared trial wave φ + χ and compute its energy as the expectation value of the Hamiltonian H divided by the norm of the trial wave. Using the symmetry of the two atoms, write the energy in terms of the on-site integral ⟨φ|H|φ⟩, the hopping integral ⟨φ|H|χ⟩ and the overlap ⟨φ|χ⟩.
chemical_bonding.name: Bonding-orbital energy of the LCAO (Hückel-type) variational treatment
chemical_bonding.form: ( mel ( φ , H , φ ) + mel ( φ , H , χ ) ) / ( 1 + braket ( φ , χ ) )
chemical_bonding.ask: With α = ⟨φ|H|φ⟩ = −13.6 eV, β = ⟨φ|H|χ⟩ = −10 eV and overlap S = 0.25, find how far the bonding orbital lies below a lone atomic orbital: α − E.
chemical_bonding.method: Expand ⟨φ+χ|H|φ+χ⟩ / ⟨φ+χ|φ+χ⟩; with normalised, identical orbitals the numerator is 2(α+β) and the denominator 2(1+S).

tachyonics.goal: A hypothetical particle has a mass that is purely imaginary, m = iμ with μ real. Write the square of its energy from the invariant that relates energy, momentum p and mass for any free particle, keeping the imaginary mass explicitly.
tachyonics.name: Mass-shell relation for imaginary (tachyonic) mass
tachyonics.ask: Its speed is v = pc²/E, so (v/c)² = p²c²/E² = 1 + μ²c⁴/E². Find (v/c)² for a particle with μc² = 3 GeV and E = 4 GeV (μ and E below are in GeV).

vars.μ: real mass scale, m = iμ (here μc² in GeV)

tachyonics.method: Start from E² − p²c² = m²c⁴ and substitute m = iμ; the sign of the mass term flips, so the speed is always above c.

formal_logic.goal: A truth function of n propositional variables is fixed by its truth table, which has 2ⁿ rows. Count all possible truth functions by grouping them according to how many rows are true: choose which k of the rows are true, and add over every possible k.
formal_logic.name: Counting Boolean functions (binomial sum over truth tables)
formal_logic.form: sum ( k , 0 , 2 ^ n , binom ( 2 ^ n , k ) )
formal_logic.ask: The binomial sum collapses to 2^(2ⁿ). Find how many distinct truth functions exist on n = 3 variables.
formal_logic.method: Each subset of the 2ⁿ rows is the set of rows where the function is true; count subsets of each size with a binomial coefficient.

molecular_biology.goal: Self-copying molecules in a sealed vessel multiply in proportion to how many copies already exist, with per-copy rate r. But the vessel holds only enough nucleotides for K copies, so copying slows as the population fills the available capacity. Write the rate of change of the number of copies N.
molecular_biology.name: Logistic growth equation (Verhulst)
molecular_biology.ask: The solution is N(t) = K / (1 + (K/N0 − 1)e^{−rt}). Starting from N0 = 10 copies with capacity K = 1000 and r = 0.5 per hour, find N after t = 10 hours.
molecular_biology.method: Exponential growth rN multiplied by the fraction of capacity still free, 1 − N/K.

topology.goal: In a two-dimensional insulator each filled electron band carries a Berry-type curvature Ω(k) over crystal momentum space. Write the transverse conductance as the conductance quantum times the integer obtained by integrating that curvature over the whole periodic momentum cell and dividing by 2π.
topology.name: TKNN formula (quantised Hall conductance from the Chern number)
topology.form: e ^ 2 / ( 2 * π * h ) * iint ( Ω , BZ )
topology.ask: The integral is 2π times an integer ν. Find the Hall conductance in siemens for ν = 2.

vars.Ω: curvature of the filled bands in momentum space
vars.BZ: the periodic momentum cell of the crystal

topology.method: The curvature integrated over a closed surface (the momentum torus) is quantised in units of 2π; multiply by e²/h.

chronodynamics.goal: An observable A may depend explicitly on time, and the state evolves under the Hamiltonian H. Write the rate of change of the expectation value ⟨A⟩: one part comes from how A fails to commute with the energy, the other from A's own explicit time dependence.
chronodynamics.name: Heisenberg equation of motion for expectation values (Ehrenfest form)
chronodynamics.form: i / ħ * avg ( comm ( H , A ) ) + avg ( pd ( A , t ) )
chronodynamics.ask: Combining this with the uncertainty relation ΔA·ΔE ≥ ½|⟨[A,H]⟩| gives ΔE·τ ≥ ħ/2, where τ = ΔA / |d⟨A⟩/dt| is the time for A to change noticeably. Find the minimum energy spread (eV) of a state that changes in τ = Δt = 1 fs, with ħ = 0.658 eV fs.
chronodynamics.method: Differentiate ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩ with the product rule and use iħ ∂|ψ⟩/∂t = H|ψ⟩ for the state and its adjoint.

particle_physics.goal: A charged particle of charge q flies through an electric field E⃗ and a magnetic field B⃗ at velocity v⃗. Write the rate of change of its relativistic momentum γmv⃗ as the sum of the electric push and the sideways magnetic push.
particle_physics.name: Lorentz force law (relativistic)
particle_physics.lhs: d ( γ * m * vec ( v ) , t )
particle_physics.form: q * vec ( E ) + q * vec ( v ) × vec ( B )
particle_physics.ask: In a pure magnetic field the momentum turns on a circle of radius R = p/(qB); for a unit charge with p in GeV/c and B in tesla this is R = p / (0.3 B) metres. Find R for p = 7000 GeV/c protons in an 8.33 T dipole.
particle_physics.method: The electric force is qE⃗; the magnetic force is the charge times the cross product of velocity with the field.

complex_analysis.goal: A complex number has modulus r and argument θ, and you want every complex w with wⁿ equal to it. Write the k-th such root in polar form, remembering that the argument is only defined up to whole turns of 2π.
complex_analysis.name: De Moivre formula for the n-th roots
complex_analysis.form: root ( n , r ) * exp ( i * ( θ + 2 * π * k ) / n )
complex_analysis.ask: Find the imaginary part of the root w₁ (k = 1) of the cube roots (n = 3) of the number with r = 8 and θ = 0.
complex_analysis.method: Write the number as r·e^{i(θ+2πk)}, take the n-th root of the modulus and divide the argument by n.

number_theory.goal: Every whole number factors into primes in exactly one way. Use that to rewrite the series of 1/nˢ over all positive integers as a product, one factor for each prime p_k, where each factor is the geometric series of all powers of that prime.
number_theory.name: Euler product formula for the zeta function
number_theory.ask: The pole of this function at s = 1, and the absence of zeros on the line Re s = 1, give the prime count π(x) ≈ x / ln x. Estimate the number of primes below x = 1 000 000.
number_theory.method: Multiply out the product: choosing one power from each prime's series gives each integer's factorisation exactly once.

set_theory.goal: A set S has n elements. Count its subsets by size with binomial coefficients and add them up. Then the collection of all those subsets is itself a set: count ITS subsets the same way, with the inner count used as the size.
set_theory.name: Cardinality of the iterated power set (binomial sums)
set_theory.form: sum ( j , 0 , sum ( k , 0 , n , binom ( n , k ) ) , binom ( sum ( k , 0 , n , binom ( n , k ) ) , j ) )
set_theory.ask: Each binomial sum collapses to a power of two, giving 2^(2ⁿ). Find the size of the power set of the power set of a 4-element set.

vars.N: number of subsets of the set of subsets
vars.k: size of a subset of S
vars.j: size of a set of subsets

set_theory.method: Σₖ C(n,k) counts all subsets; the outer sum does the same for a set whose size is that inner sum.

temporal_mechanics.goal: A gas is released into a larger container and its microstates spread out. Before, microstate j had probability q_j; afterwards it has probability p_j. Write the change in entropy as the statistical entropy of the final distribution minus that of the initial one, each built from the probabilities and their logarithms.
temporal_mechanics.name: Gibbs entropy change (statistical arrow of time)
temporal_mechanics.form: - kB * sumk ( j , p _ j * ln ( p _ j ) ) + kB * sumk ( j , q _ j * ln ( q _ j ) )
temporal_mechanics.ask: For an ideal gas filling all accessible states equally, this becomes nR ln(V₂/V₁). Find the entropy increase when n = 2 mol expands freely from V₁ = 1 L to V₂ = 3 L.
temporal_mechanics.method: Each microstate contributes −kB·p·ln p; subtract the initial sum from the final one.

assembly_lines.goal: A line of k stations processes components one after another; station s takes time t_s. The first component must pass through every station, and after that a new component leaves each time the slowest station, with time τ, finishes one. Write the total time to finish N components.
assembly_lines.name: Pipeline makespan (fill time plus bottleneck throughput)
assembly_lines.form: sum ( s , 1 , k , t _ s ) + ( N - 1 ) * τ
assembly_lines.ask: If every station takes the same time t, the total is (k + N − 1)·t. Find T for k = 8 stations, N = 1000 components and t = 0.5 s.
assembly_lines.method: Fill the line once (sum of the station times), then one more component per bottleneck cycle for the remaining N − 1.

cpt_symmetry.goal: Find the first-order relativistic wave equation for a spin-½ field ψ of mass m: it is linear in the spacetime derivatives ∂_μ, which are contracted with four matrices γ^μ, and its square must reproduce E² = p²c² + m²c⁴. Its negative-energy solutions predicted the existence of antimatter. Write the expression that must vanish.
cpt_symmetry.name: Dirac equation
cpt_symmetry.form: i * ħ * γ ^ μ * ∂ _ μ * ψ - m * c * ψ
cpt_symmetry.ask: An electron and a positron at rest annihilate into two photons, each carrying mc², so each has wavelength h/(mc). Find it in pm with h in 1e-34 J s, m in 1e-31 kg and c in 1e8 m/s.
cpt_symmetry.method: Take the square root of the energy-momentum relation with operators E → iħ∂_t, p → −iħ∇; it only works if the coefficients anticommute, i.e. are matrices.

special_relativity.goal: A body of rest mass m moves at speed v. Write its total energy as the rest-mass energy multiplied by the time-dilation factor, written out in full in terms of v and c.
special_relativity.name: Relativistic energy (mass-energy equivalence)
special_relativity.ask: Find the total energy of m = 1 kg moving at 0.6c, with c in units of 1e8 m/s (so v = 1.8) - the answer is in 1e16 J.
special_relativity.method: The energy is the time component of the four-momentum, γmc², with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).

dyson_swarm.goal: A collector far from a star sees its disc fill a cone of half-angle θ_s around the line of sight. Every direction inside that cone delivers the star's surface radiance B. Write the power per unit area falling on a collector facing the star by integrating the radiance, projected onto the collector's normal, over the solid angle of the cone.
dyson_swarm.name: Irradiance from a uniform stellar disc (radiance integrated over solid angle)
dyson_swarm.form: int ( 0 , 2 * π , int ( 0 , θ _ s , B * cos ( θ ) * sin ( θ ) , θ ) , φ )
dyson_swarm.ask: The integral gives πB·sin²θ_s = σT⁴(R/r)² = L/(4πr²). Find the flux at r = 1.496e11 m from a star of luminosity L = 3.828e26 W.

vars.θ: angle from the line of sight
vars.φ: azimuth around the line of sight
vars.s: label: the edge of the stellar disc

dyson_swarm.method: In spherical angles the solid-angle element is sinθ dθ dφ; the flat collector picks up a cosθ projection factor.

protein_folding.goal: A protein chain can sit in any of an enormous number of conformations j, each with energy E_j, in contact with a heat bath at temperature T. Write the probability that it is found in its native conformation N, weighting each conformation by its thermal factor and normalising by the sum over all of them.
protein_folding.name: Boltzmann probability of the native state (canonical ensemble)
protein_folding.form: exp ( - E _ N / ( kB * T ) ) / sumk ( j , exp ( - E _ j / ( kB * T ) ) )
protein_folding.ask: Model the chain as n = 10 residues with k = 3 states each: the native state lies at energy 0 and the other kⁿ − 1 conformations all lie Δ higher, with Δ/(kB·T) = x = 15. Find the probability of the native state.
protein_folding.method: Each state is weighted by e^{−E/kBT}; dividing by the sum of all weights makes the probabilities add to one.

xenobiology.goal: An alien genome is a string of L letters drawn from an alphabet of b chemically distinct bases, base j appearing with probability p_j. Write the information it can store, in bits: the length times the average surprise per letter, built from the probabilities and their logarithms, converted from natural units to bits.
xenobiology.name: Shannon entropy of a genome sequence
xenobiology.form: - L * sum ( j , 1 , b , p _ j * ln ( p _ j ) / ln ( 2 ) )
xenobiology.ask: For equally likely bases p_j = 1/b this becomes L·log₂ b. Find the information in bits of a 100-letter genome over an 8-letter alphabet.
xenobiology.method: Average −log₂ p_j over the alphabet; log₂ p = ln p / ln 2; multiply by the number of letters.

neurobiology.goal: Ions of valence z and concentration C(x) cross a cell membrane. They drift down their concentration gradient with diffusion constant D, and are also pushed by the electric field from the membrane potential V(x). Write the ion flux j as the sum of both effects, using the thermal energy per mole RT and the charge per mole zF.
neurobiology.name: Nernst–Planck equation (electrodiffusion flux)
neurobiology.form: - D * ( d ( C , x ) + z * F / ( R * T ) * C * d ( V , x ) )
neurobiology.expr: R * T / F * ln ( Ci / Co )
neurobiology.ask: Setting j = 0 and integrating across the membrane gives the equilibrium potential; for K⁺ (z = 1) its magnitude is (RT/F)·ln(C_in/C_out). Find it in volts at T = 310 K with 140 mM inside and 5 mM outside.
neurobiology.method: Fick's diffusion term −D dC/dx plus electrical drift whose mobility is related to D by the thermal energy RT.

quantum_foam.goal: Empty space is a sea of field modes; each mode of wavenumber k keeps a ground-state energy ½ħω even with no particles present. For a field of mass m, ω depends on k through the relativistic energy relation. Sum the ground-state energies of all modes per unit volume, counting modes in spherical shells of k-space, up to a cutoff wavenumber k_P where spacetime itself stops being smooth.
quantum_foam.name: Zero-point vacuum energy density (massive field, Planck cutoff)
quantum_foam.ask: The same fluctuations let a particle-antiparticle pair borrow ΔE = 2mc² for Δt ≈ ħ/(2ΔE) = ħ/(4mc²). Find Δt for an electron pair in zeptoseconds, with ħ = 658.2 keV·zs, m = 511 keV/c² and c = 1.
quantum_foam.method: Modes per unit volume in a shell are 4πk² dk/(2π)³; each carries ½ħω with ħω = √(ħ²c²k² + m²c⁴).

causality_violation.goal: A signal is sent faster than light: it covers a distance Δx in time Δt. An observer moves at speed v along the same line. Write the time between emission and reception as that observer measures it, using the full transformation between the two frames with the time-dilation factor written out.
causality_violation.name: Lorentz transformation of a time interval
causality_violation.expr: ( v * Δx / c ^ 2 - Δt ) / sqrt ( 1 - v ^ 2 / c ^ 2 )
causality_violation.ask: When vΔx/c² > Δt the result is negative: the moving observer sees the signal arrive before it was sent. Take c = 1, a signal at three times light speed (Δt = 1 s, Δx = 3 light-seconds) and v = 0.5; find by how much it arrives before it was sent.
causality_violation.method: Mix time and space so that c²t² − x² is unchanged; the relative weight of x in the new time is v/c².

supersymmetry.goal: Stable heavy particles of number density n fill the early universe, which expands at rate H. They annihilate in pairs with velocity-averaged cross-section σv and are re-created from the thermal bath, which by itself would hold the equilibrium density n_eq. Write the rate of change of n including dilution by expansion in three dimensions.
supersymmetry.name: Boltzmann equation for relic abundance (thermal freeze-out)
supersymmetry.ask: Solving it through freeze-out gives Ωh² ≈ 0.1 × (3e-26 cm³/s)/⟨σv⟩. With ⟨σv⟩ = s × 1e-26 cm³/s for s = 2 and Hubble parameter h = 0.7, find the relic density Ω.
supersymmetry.method: Volume dilution gives −3Hn; annihilation goes as n², and inverse production must cancel it exactly when n = n_eq.

black_hole_interior.goal: A body is at rest at the horizon of a non-rotating black hole of mass M, at radius 2GM/c², and falls straight in. Inside the horizon its radial speed obeys (dr/dτ)² = c²(2GM/(c²r) − 1). Write the proper time from the horizon to the centre as an integral over r.
black_hole_interior.name: Maximal infall proper time inside a Schwarzschild horizon
black_hole_interior.ask: The integral evaluates to π r_s/(2c) = πGM/c³. Find it in seconds for M = 1.989e31 kg, with G = 6.674e-11 and c = 2.998e8 (SI).
black_hole_interior.method: Solve the radial equation for dτ = dr / |dr/dτ| and integrate from r = 0 to the horizon; substitute r = r_s sin²(η/2).

multiverse.goal: A homogeneous universe with scale factor a(t) contains matter-energy of density ρ, has spatial curvature k and a constant vacuum energy Λ. Write the square of its relative expansion rate from energy conservation in general relativity.
multiverse.name: Friedmann equation with cosmological constant
multiverse.ask: When Λ dominates, ȧ/a = H is constant and a ∝ e^{Ht}, so a region's volume - and the number of Hubble volumes it holds - grows as e^{3Ht}. Find that factor after H·t = 2 (H = 0.5, t = 4 in matching units).
multiverse.method: Apply Einstein's equations to the uniform metric (or Newtonian energy of an expanding sphere plus curvature and vacuum terms).

simulation_hypothesis.goal: Any region that holds information must hold it in physical states, and a finite region with finite energy has finitely many. Write the maximum number of bits that fit in a sphere of radius R as 2πR/(ħc·ln 2) times its total energy, with that energy written as the volume integral (in spherical shells) of the mass density ρ(r) times c².
simulation_hypothesis.name: Bekenstein bound (energy integrated over the region)
simulation_hypothesis.ask: With the energy integral done, I = 2πRE/(ħc ln 2). Find the bound for a proton: R = 0.84 fm, E = 938.3 MeV and ħc = 197.3 MeV fm.
simulation_hypothesis.method: Entropy over kB is at most 2πRE/(ħc); bits are entropy divided by ln 2; a sphere's volume element is 4πr² dr.

axiom_theory.goal: Encode a proof - a sequence of m formulas, formula j being a string of n_j symbols with codes a_jk - as one whole number. Encode each formula as a product of successive primes p_k raised to the symbol codes; then encode the sequence the same way, with successive primes raised to the formulas' own numbers.
axiom_theory.name: Gödel numbering of a proof (prime-power encoding)
axiom_theory.form: prod ( j , 1 , m , p _ j ^ prod ( k , 1 , n _ j , p _ k ^ ( a _ ( j * k ) ) ) )
axiom_theory.ask: Find the number of a single formula of three symbols whose codes are a = 3, b = 1 and c = 2 (the inner product, with primes 2, 3, 5).

vars.a: symbol code (a_jk; in step 2 the first code)

axiom_theory.method: Unique prime factorisation makes the encoding reversible: read off exponents to recover each symbol, then each formula.

theory_of_everything.goal: Write one action for everything known: spacetime curvature with a vacuum energy, the gauge fields with field strength F_μν, matter fermions ψ moving through the gauge-covariant derivative D_μ, and the scalar field φ whose potential has its minimum at |φ| = v. Integrate the sum of all their Lagrangian densities over spacetime with the invariant volume factor built from the metric determinant g.
theory_of_everything.name: Einstein–Hilbert + Standard Model action (core theory)
theory_of_everything.form: int ( sqrt ( - g ) * ( c ^ 4 / ( 16 * π * G ) * ( R - 2 * Λ ) - 1 / 4 * F _ μν * F ^ μν + bar ( ψ ) * ( i * ħ * c * γ ^ μ * D _ μ - m * c ^ 2 ) * ψ + abs ( D _ μ * φ ) ^ 2 - λ * ( abs ( φ ) ^ 2 - v ^ 2 ) ^ 2 ) , x )
theory_of_everything.ask: The couplings in this action run with energy. At one loop 1/α(Q) = 1/α(M) + b/(2π)·ln(Q/M). Starting from the strong coupling α = 0.118 at M = 91.19 GeV with b = 7, find 1/α at the unification scale Q = 2e16 GeV.
theory_of_everything.method: Gravity enters as curvature R − 2Λ, gauge fields as −¼F², fermions through the Dirac operator, the scalar through |Dφ|² minus a double-well potential; √−g makes the volume element invariant.

omnilex.goal: To predict everything, add up every possible history. Slice the time from start to end into N steps of length ε; at each intermediate step the particle of mass m may be at any position x_k. Weight each zig-zag path by the phase e^{iS/ħ}, where S is the discretised action (kinetic minus potential energy V_k at each slice, times ε), integrate over all intermediate positions with the proper normalising factor per slice, and let the slicing become infinitely fine.
omnilex.name: Feynman path integral (time-sliced propagator)
omnilex.ask: For a free particle the sum over paths gives K = √(m/(2πiħT))·e^{imL²/(2ħT)}: only the classical path's phase survives. Find that phase mL²/(2ħT) in radians for an electron (m = 9.109e-31 kg) crossing L = 1e-6 m in T = 1e-9 s, with ħ = 1.055e-34 J s.

vars.x: positions x_k (integrated over every intermediate one)

omnilex.method: Split e^{−iHT/ħ} into N factors, insert a complete set of position states between each pair, and do the Gaussian momentum integral at each slice.
